newsitem.title: UK: Wet Brent bid firmer, but paper market unmoved.
newsitem.headline: Wet Brent bid firmer, but paper market unmoved.

text.p: The North Sea physical Brent crude market was bid sharply higher on Thursday although the cash market failed to respond, hanging around Wednesday's traded levels in thin talk, traders said.
A dealer at a Swiss-based trading house confirmed that he was bidding at July Brent -55 cents for a Brent cargo loading in the June 22-26 window.
The bid is 15 cents up on a deal done on Wednesday for a June 17-19 loader.
"We've had only very high offers...mostly Dated-related," the bidder said.

Although shipping fixtures revealed that Brent is starting to head transatlantic again, and a raft of North Sea deals on Wednesday sharply eased the June overhang, some traders were puzzled at the market's apparent leap.
"It looks to me like some sort of CFD play," said one trader.
But the paper market was unmoved with CFDs for next week (June 16-20) slipping slightly to talk at August Brent -70/-66, and the following week (June 23-27) at August -58/-56.
Intermonth spreads were little changed with July/August talked at -32/-30 and August/September at -25/-20.
At least ten North Sea cargoes, mostly Statfjords and Ekofisks, found homes on Wednesday, shrinking the June overhang of non-Brent cargoes to around a dozen.
A steep market contango has encouraged buying for storage, dealers said.
"A lot was cleared out yesterday and (producers) have been doing more quietly for the last week," said one. "The market looks a bit healthier."
Despite a narrow transatlantic arbitrage, a ULCC of Brent crude has been fixed to move to the U.S. on June 17, while a Suezmax has been fixed for the end of the month.
The premium for July WTI over July Brent was around $1.20 a barrel on Thursday, having slipped as low as $1.00 earlier in the week.
Two Brent cargoes, loading June 27-29, were due to be nominated from the paper chains on Thursday according to the original programme.
North Sea trading was expected to be fairly quiet for the rest of the week, with many traders attending a gathering in Norway.
